big_idea: The same number can be shown many ways: numerals, words, ten-frames, base-ten rods, tally marks.
learning_intention: We are learning to read and represent any number to 50 in five different forms.
student_learning_goal: I can read and represent numbers to 50 in many ways and tell where I see numbers in everyday life.
success_criteria: I can read a number from 0 to 50 written as a numeral or in words.
I can show the same number with ten-frames, base-ten rods, or tally marks.
I can name a place I see numbers used in real life.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Five Ways to Show a Number' with 5 columns: Numeral / Word / Ten-Frames / Base-Ten Rods / Tally

OPTIONAL: Lila and Otto — if available; otherwise teacher voices both characters in two distinct voices, or substitutes two stuffed animals / paper-bag puppets / pictures on the anchor poster. Activity is unaffected.
Sample number-friend gallery card (32) showing all 5 forms
Lesson 2 formative tracker (Representations) — provided in assessment_suite stage
Number-Word Match Cards (M7) — 1 set per pair

minds_on.hook: Otto found the number 32 written in five different places yesterday. Can you spot how they all mean the same thing? Scoot scampers to the chart: 'Numbers tell stories — show me yours!'
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Hold up Otto and a sample gallery card showing the number 32 in five forms.

'Friends — Otto was looking around our school yesterday and noticed something. The same number — THIRTY-TWO — was written in FIVE different ways!' Hold up the gallery card.

Go through each form: 'Here's the NUMERAL: 32. Here's the WORD: thirty-two. Here are TEN-FRAMES showing 32 — see, three full frames and two extras. Here are BASE-TEN RODS showing 32 — three ten-rods and two single ones. And here are TALLY MARKS — count them in groups of 5.' Pause. 'All five mean the SAME amount. Today we are going to be Number Friends Detectives — we'll find the same number written in different ways and match them up.'
student_actions: Look at the gallery card without speaking.
Identify each of the five forms aloud as the teacher names it.

steps.instruction: Set up 5 gallery stations around the classroom. Each station has cards for 6 different numbers (e.g. 7, 12, 25, 33, 41, 49) but ONLY in one form: Station A numerals, Station B words, Station C ten-frames, Station D base-ten rods, Station E tally marks. Pairs rotate through each station carrying a recording sheet, write down which number they see at each station.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'You and your partner are Number Detectives. At each gallery station, you'll see 6 numbers shown ONE way. Write down what each number is on your sheet. By the end, you'll have seen the same 6 numbers shown 5 different ways.' Demonstrate at Station A.

steps.instruction: Mid-rotation pause: bring children back to the carpet. Hold up a card from Station C (ten-frames) showing 25. Ask 'how do you read this?' Take responses. Connect to Station A's numeral. 'Same number. Different way of showing it.'
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Quick stop. Look at this ten-frame card.' Hold up 25 (two full frames + 5 in a third). 'How do we know it's twenty-five and not thirty?' Lead them to count: 'Two full frames is 20, plus 5 more is 25.' Repeat with another card.

steps.instruction: Send pairs back to finish the rotations. Use the tracker to record which children can read all 5 forms confidently. Stretch round: at Station E (tally marks), some pairs get a 'mystery card' with the number 50 in tally — counting that many marks is genuinely hard.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Last rotation. When you finish, bring your sheet to me — we'll check it together at the carpet.' Walk around. Note which children read each form independently.

steps.instruction: Real-life Number Hunt. Send children to walk the classroom and find numbers in real use (clock, calendar, page numbers, height chart, supplies labels). Each child names ONE place where a number is used and tells the class what JOB that number does.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Numbers are everywhere in our classroom. Find ONE place where a number is used. Bring a sticky-note. Tell me: where is the number, and what JOB does it do?' Take 6-8 examples (clock = telling time; page = labelling; height chart = measuring; recycling bin = counting; etc.).

steps.instruction: Closing chart-build. Bring children back. Build the 'Five Ways to Show a Number' anchor chart together. Each column gets one example of a number shown in that form. Children volunteer the examples from their gallery walks.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Help me fill in our anchor chart. What number should we use as our example?' Take a class vote (often 25 or 30). Fill in all 5 columns together. Display.

differentiation.for_emerging: These children stay at Stations A (numerals) and B (words) for both rotations and skip C-D-E. Reading numerals and words is the foundation; the multi-representation work comes once that's fluent.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch cards at every station: numbers 50-99 written in each form (e.g. 73 in tally marks). Note: B1.1 caps at 50; this is genuine stretch into Grade 2 territory.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a number-name reference card (numerals + words + a small ten-frame for each number). Allow children to draw their answers rather than write words. Pair with a strong-reader peer.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Real-life Number Hunt (Step 4) gets extended: these children walk a longer route around the school (with adult supervision) and bring back 5+ found numbers. Body-on-floor exploration is the strongest learning path.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Can the child read each of the 5 forms independently? Can they connect different representations of the same number? Can they name a real-life number-use?
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the tracker per child as you observe at each station. The 5 form-columns capture B1.1 explicitly.

discussion_prompts: Which form was easiest to read for you? Which was hardest?
Why might a teacher use base-ten rods instead of just writing the number?
Where in your home do you see numbers? What jobs do they do?
If I write FIFTY, can you also write it as a numeral? As tally marks?
consolidation.exit_routine: Teacher writes a number (e.g. 27) on the board. Each child whispers to a partner ONE other way to show it: 'twenty-seven', or 'two ten-rods + 7 ones', or 'two full ten-frames + 7 in a third', or 'tally marks in groups of 5'. Partners share with the class on the way to the door. Scoot tags out by waving the class chart: 'Numbers home, see you tomorrow!'

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Representations tracker for B1.1 (per-form per-child). Real-life number-use observation note.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: B1.1 has two parts: read numbers (passive) AND represent them (active). The tracker captures both. Children who can read all 5 forms but can't ACTIVELY produce them will struggle in Lesson 3's compose/decompose work — the base-ten and ten-frame production is critical there.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child reads ten-frames as 'just twenty' — repairing partial-frame counting
expanded_walkthrough.rationale: The most common Grade-1 trap on B1.1 with ten-frames is the child who reads 25 (two full frames + 5 in a third) as '20' — they count the full frames and stop. The third frame's 5 ones get ignored because the partial frame doesn't fit the 'each frame is 10' rule the child internalised. Step 2 (mid-rotation pause) is where this surfaces. The script below covers the precise prompt that breaks the all-or-nothing frame-reading habit.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair returns from Station C with the recording sheet showing '20' for the 25-ten-frame card. The teacher checks their sheet against the answer key during a quick walk-through. The child looks confident — they're sure 20 is right.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'Walk me through how you got 20.' The child explains: 'There are two full frames. Each frame is 10. So 10 + 10 = 20.' Affirm: 'Great math! Two full frames IS 20. But look more carefully at the card — is there ONLY two frames?' Show them again. The child notices the third partial frame. 'Right — there's a THIRD frame, but it's not full. How many dots are in it?' Wait. (5.) 'So we have 20 from the full frames PLUS 5 from the partial frame. 20 + 5 = 25. Same number, different reading.'

The critical follow-up: 'Sometimes ten-frames have partial frames. The partial frame shows the ONES. Two full frames is 20 — that's the TENS. Plus 5 ones in the partial frame. That's 25.' Connect to base-ten language: '2 tens and 5 ones = 25.'

Watch the child at the next ten-frame card. If they correctly count 32 (three full + 2 in a fourth), tick 'reads ten-frame' on the tracker. If they revert to ignoring the partial frame, they need 1:1 reteach with hands-on ten-frame manipulatives in the small-group rotation.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Reads only the full frames; ignores partial. 25 → '20'. Or 32 → '30'. Hasn't yet generalised to partial frames.
(Mid) After the partial-frame demo, reads correctly on the next card but slips on the next type of partial (e.g. correctly reads 25 = 2 full + 5 partial, but reads 32 as 30 again).
(Strong) Reads any partial-frame card by counting full frames (×10) plus the partial dots. Connects to tens-and-ones language unprompted.
(Stretched) Volunteers: 'I bet I could read 50 — that would be 5 full frames and 0 partial. Or 49 would be 4 full and 9 in a fifth.' Has internalised the structural rule.
common_misconceptions: Each ten-frame is 10. (True for full frames; the rule fails on partial frames. Repair: name the partial frame as 'the ones'.)
Numbers are written one way only. (Some children believe only the numeral or only the word counts. Repair: the gallery walk explicitly shows 5 forms.)

Tally marks count by 1s. (True for individual marks, but the diagonal marks group them by 5. Children sometimes count tally marks one-by-one and lose count past 20. Repair: count by 5s using the diagonals.)
recovery_moves: Always count ten-frames as 'tens plus ones'. Two full frames + 5 partial = 2 tens + 5 ones = 25. Make the tens-and-ones language explicit every time.
Use base-ten rod overlay. Lay 2 ten-rods next to two full ten-frames (visually identical) and 5 single ones next to the partial frame. The equivalence makes the 'partial = ones' rule physical.
Tally marks: count by 5s, not by 1s. Each diagonal mark groups a 5; children should chant '5, 10, 15, 20, 25' while pointing at each diagonal.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B1.1 — reading and representing numbers to 50 in five forms.

parts_outline.task: Three matching-grid scenes. Each scene shows a target number in one form (numeral, ten-frame, base-ten rod) and asks the child to draw OR identify the same number in another form.
Number-Word Match: 6 numerals on the left (5, 12, 25, 38, 50, 47), 6 number-words on the right in random order. The child draws lines to match.
Open prompt: 'Pick a number between 10 and 50. Show it FIVE different ways in this box: numeral, word, ten-frames, base-ten rods, tally marks.'
